title: Homology Axioms Degree and Classical Applications

items.title: Unreduced homology theory on cw pairs
items.statement: An ordinary theory on CW pairs consists of functors h_n to abelian groups for n in Z and natural boundary maps, with homotopy invariance, pair long exactness, CW excision, dimension h_n(*)=0 for n!=0, and arbitrary disjoint-union additivity. Write G=h_0(*). State CW excision as h_*(U,U intersect V) -> h_*(U union V,V) for subcomplexes; this avoids asking a CW-only functor to evaluate non-CW deleted pairs.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Definition 11.1, printed pp.25–26
May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§4, pp.110–111, CW-pair formulation

items.title: Singular homology satisfies homotopy exactness and excision
items.statement: Singular homology with any fixed abelian coefficient group satisfies the homotopy, exactness, naturality and CW excision axioms.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Definition 11.1 and ensuing verification, pp.25–26
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, pp.160–162

items.proof_strategy: Package published proofs; obtain subcomplex excision by CW collars/mapping cylinders and the open excision theorem, spelling out the neighbourhood replacement. Pair homotopy invariance also follows from absolute invariance and the natural pair LES.

items.title: Singular homology satisfies dimension and arbitrary additivity
items.statement: For arbitrary G, H_n(*;G)=G if n=0 and is zero otherwise; the canonical direct sum map for any disjoint family of pairs is an isomorphism. Thus singular homology is an ordinary theory with coefficient G.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Definition 11.1, pp.25–26

items.proof_strategy: Compute the one-generator point complex with alternating zero and identity differentials; extend the existing absolute disjoint-sum result to relative chain quotients.

items.title: Reduced homology theory and augmentation
items.statement: For nonempty based X define reduced h_n(X)=ker(h_n(X)->h_n(*)); the basepoint splits the augmentation. State reduced homotopy, exact-cofiber, wedge and dimension axioms. Keep the library convention reduced H_n(empty)=0 in all degrees; the augmented-chain convention H_-1(empty)=G is a distinct unused extension.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§4, pp.110–111
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, pp.160–161

items.title: Unreduced pair and reduced quotient axioms are equivalent on cw pairs
items.statement: On based CW spaces with basepoint a vertex, reduced theories and unreduced theories on CW pairs determine one another. For nonempty A, h_n(X,A)=reduced h_n(X/A); for A empty use X_+. Boundaries, coefficient identifications, natural transformations and arbitrary wedge/disjoint-sum axioms correspond.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§4, CW definition and theorem, pp.110–111
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, pp.160–162

items.proof_strategy: Use topological mapping cylinder and cone constructions explicitly; HEP identifies cofibers with quotients. Derive the pair LES and CW excision from reduced cofiber exactness using mapping-cone quotients, and the converse by pair exactness. Establish triple exactness here for subsequent skeletal diagrams. Include natural suspension and boundary-as-desuspension of the cofiber map; no weak-equivalence axiom outside CW pairs.

items.title: Coefficient normalized morphism of ordinary homology theories
items.statement: A morphism is a graded natural transformation on CW pairs commuting with connecting maps. It is normalized by a specified homomorphism h_0(*) -> k_0(*); a comparison equivalence is normalized by a specified coefficient isomorphism.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, pp.119–120, natural comparison and boundary compatibility
references.locator: 15§2, pp.119–120, natural comparison and boundary compatibility

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, p.161, uniqueness with coefficients
references.locator: Axioms for Homology, p.161, uniqueness with coefficients

items.title: Any ordinary homology theory computes relative cell groups from its coefficient group
items.statement: For every ordinary h, h_k(D^n,S^{n-1}) is G for k=n and zero otherwise. For n=0 interpret the pair as (*,empty). Chosen ordered disk orientations fix these identifications; reduced h_k(S^n) is G in degree n, including S^0.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§3, suspension corollaries, p.109; 15§2 p.120

items.proof_strategy: Use the cone LES and natural suspension repeatedly, starting with h_0(S^0,one point)=G. Negative-degree vanishing follows by dimension, not by imposing an extra connective axiom.

items.title: Any ordinary homology theory has a cellular chain complex on a cw pair
items.statement: For a CW pair let F_n=A union X^n and F_-1=A. Then C_n^h(X,A)=h_n(F_n,F_{n-1}) is the direct sum of a copy of G for each relative n-cell. The successive boundary composites d_n have d_(n-1)d_n=0 and are natural for cellular maps.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, definition of C_n and d, p.119
references.locator: 15§2, definition of C_n and d, p.119

items.proof_strategy: Use quotient wedges, arbitrary additivity, and exactness of triples. Do not yet identify the integer incidence action for an arbitrary h.

items.title: Finite dimensional skeletal exactness computes axiomatic homology
items.statement: For finite-dimensional CW pairs, h_n(X,A) is naturally isomorphic, for cellular maps, to H_n(C_*^h(X,A)). The isomorphism commutes with pair boundaries and is forced by the skeletal exact diagram. It does not require finitely many cells.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, second theorem and full exact-diagram proof, pp.119–120
references.locator: 15§2, second theorem and full exact-diagram proof, pp.119–120

items.proof_strategy: Induct on dimension to prove vanishing above dimension and stabilization below the attaching dimension. In the three-skeleton diagram send x to the class of rho(y) for any skeletal lift y; check existence, independence, inverse and pair-boundary compatibility. Stop the stabilization at the finite top dimension; no colimit assertion is used here.

items.title: Oriented simplex comparison for an ordinary homology theory
items.statement: For finite simplicial pairs (K,L), oriented simplex generators identify C_*^h(K,L) with C_*^simp(K,L;Z) tensor G, including alternating face signs; hence give a coefficient-normalized comparison h_n(K,L) -> H_n(K,L;G), natural for simplicial maps.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, both cellular comparison theorems, pp.119–120
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §2C, Theorem 2C.1 setting, pp.177–179

items.proof_strategy: Define the relative class of an ordered simplex recursively by its boundary and base coefficient; prove adjacent transpositions reverse it. The relative boundary lands in the alternating sum of face classes by naturality/excision. Degenerate simplicial images factor through a lower-dimensional simplex. Compare the resulting explicit complex with published simplicial/singular homology; no tensor-exactness assumption on G.

items.title: Finite simplicial approximation for homology comparison
items.statement: For finite simplicial pairs (K,L),(P,Q), every continuous map of their realizations has, after enough common barycentric subdivision of K and L, a simplicial approximation through a homotopy of pairs.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §2C, Lemma 2C.2 and Theorem 2C.1, pp.177–179

items.proof_strategy: Prove the open-star criterion, choose stars for vertices in L from Q and then extend their open preimages to a neighbourhood of L. Finiteness and a Lebesgue number make all sufficiently small stars subordinate, with these constrained choices at L. The straight-line homotopy stays in a common target simplex and in Q on L. This is the finite-pair specialization, not cellular approximation.

items.title: Subdivision compatible continuous polyhedral homology comparison
items.statement: The oriented-simplex comparison is independent of finite subdivision and natural for all continuous maps of finite simplicial pairs; it commutes with pair connecting maps.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, exact-diagram naturality and boundary compatibility, pp.119–120
references.locator: 15§2, exact-diagram naturality and boundary compatibility, pp.119–120

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2C.1 and proof, pp.177–179

items.proof_strategy: For the identity from the old triangulation to its subdivision, each old skeleton lies in the new skeleton. Show the relative class of an old simplex maps to the sum of its consistently oriented subdivided simplices: induction on dimension identifies the boundary, and injectivity of the relative-simplex boundary fixes the class (dimension zero is the coefficient map). Apply the skeletal exact diagram. Then replace a continuous map by a simplicial approximation; homotopy invariance proves naturality and independence of all choices.

items.title: Cw homotopy equivalence inclusions are strong deformation retracts
items.statement: If A is a CW subcomplex of X and A -> X is a homotopy equivalence, then X strongly deformation retracts onto A. Homotopic attaching maps along a CW pair give homotopy-equivalent adjunction spaces relative to their common target.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Propositions 0.18–0.19 and Corollary 0.20, complete proofs pp.16–17
references.locator: Propositions 0.18–0.19 and Corollary 0.20, complete proofs pp.16–17

items.proof_strategy: Prove the relative inverse lemma inline: extend the inverse homotopy to make it fix A; cancel the retraced restriction by an HEP homotopy of homotopies. Apply to the inclusion. For attachment invariance use the homotopy attaching cylinder and its two relative deformation retractions.

items.title: Finite cw pairs admit finite simplicial homotopy models
items.statement: Every finite CW pair is homotopy equivalent as a pair to a finite simplicial pair.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2C.5, construction and proof pp.182–184

items.proof_strategy: Build Hatcher simplicial M(f) over each simplex by coning M(f restricted to boundary), retaining the target and barycentrically subdivided domain. Contractibility plus the previous HEP lemma supplies the retraction, then adjust its endpoint to f. Build C(f) by adjoining the cone on the domain. First model A, then attach the finitely many cells of X outside A; keep both A-models in the common double-cylinder construction. Check every retraction preserves the designated subpair. This proves the pair version rather than assuming that separate models for X and A are compatible.

items.title: Coefficient comparison on finite cw pairs
items.statement: A specified coefficient isomorphism determines a unique boundary-compatible natural equivalence between ordinary homology theories on finite CW pairs.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, uniqueness theorem pp.119–120
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2C.5 pp.182–184; Axioms for Homology p.161
references.locator: Theorem 2C.5 pp.182–184; Axioms for Homology p.161

items.proof_strategy: Compare each theory with simplicial chains using the specified coefficients and transport along a finite simplicial homotopy model. Independence and continuous naturality follow by comparing two models via their homotopy equivalences and the continuous polyhedral comparison. A normalized natural morphism is forced on relative simplices by boundaries, then on the exact diagram, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Sphere endomorphisms act by the same integer in every ordinary theory
items.statement: If u:S^n -> S^n induces multiplication by d on reduced integral singular homology, it induces d times the identity on reduced h_n(S^n)=G in every ordinary theory. This includes n=0 using reduced H_0 and the chosen difference generator.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, first theorem and coefficient paragraph p.119
references.locator: 15§2, first theorem and coefficient paragraph p.119

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 4.59 homology argument, printed pp.399–401 (in chapter 4); alternative simplicial route specified in notes
references.locator: Theorem 4.59 homology argument, printed pp.399–401 (in chapter 4); alternative simplicial route specified in notes

items.proof_strategy: Apply finite CW comparison with singular coefficients G; on simplicial sphere chains the fundamental cycle gives the tensor G generator and the same integer action. Do not invoke the homotopy classification of sphere maps.

items.title: Axiomatic cellular boundaries are integral incidence matrices with coefficients
items.statement: For arbitrary G, C_*^h(X,A) has differential given by the published integral incidence matrix acting on G. In dimension one use signed endpoints. Thus C_*^h is canonically C_*^cell(X,A;Z) tensor G after cell orientations are chosen.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, first theorem and arbitrary-coefficient paragraph p.119
references.locator: 15§2, first theorem and arbitrary-coefficient paragraph p.119

items.proof_strategy: Project the attaching boundary onto each target cell sphere and use natural suspension/cofiber boundaries and the sphere-action lemma. Arbitrary additivity gives column-finite direct sums. This supplies the coefficient-matrix step missing from a bare five-lemma proof.

items.title: Finite dimensional axiomatic homology has finite subcomplex support
items.statement: For finite-dimensional CW pairs, the canonical colimit over finite subcomplexes K of X of h_n(K,K intersect A) maps isomorphically to h_n(X,A).

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, cellular calculation pp.119–120
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Lemma 2.34 p.138, finite support reasoning

items.proof_strategy: Cellular chains are direct sums. Each cycle and each boundary witness has finite support contained, by closure finiteness, in a finite subcomplex. Use the natural skeletal isomorphism for subcomplex inclusions. Compact images will subsequently ensure compatibility under continuous maps; singular-chain support is not being assumed for h.

items.title: A comparison isomorphism propagates over one skeleton stage
items.statement: Given an existing natural morphism of ordinary theories commuting with the pair LES, if its components on the previous skeleton and the relative n-cell groups are isomorphisms in every degree, its components on the next skeleton are isomorphisms.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, skeletal exactness pp.119–120
Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Proposition 9.6, opening p.22

items.proof_strategy: Apply the five lemma to five consecutive terms in the commuting pair LES. This propagates invertibility of constructed maps; it does not construct a natural transformation from an abstract coefficient isomorphism.

items.title: Eilenberg steenrod uniqueness on finite dimensional cw pairs
items.statement: A specified coefficient isomorphism determines a unique natural equivalence of ordinary theories on finite-dimensional CW pairs, commuting with boundaries. Infinitely many cells in a bounded range of dimensions are allowed.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 15§2, pp.119–120

items.proof_strategy: Pass the finite-CW comparisons through finite-subcomplex colimits. Every continuous map takes a finite subcomplex into a finite subcomplex, so the extension is natural for all maps, not just cellular maps. Uniqueness and boundary compatibility follow on each finite support.

items.title: Ordinary homology theories have mayer vietoris for cw covers
items.statement: For CW subcomplexes U,V with X=U union V, any ordinary theory has the natural Mayer–Vietoris exact sequence with maps (i_*,-j_*) and sum, also for CW pairs covered by subpairs.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, Mayer–Vietoris derivation p.162
references.locator: Axioms for Homology, Mayer–Vietoris derivation p.162

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Lemma 11.6, pp.27–28
May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§5, first Mayer–Vietoris theorem pp.112–113

items.proof_strategy: Derive the relative excision isomorphism and compare the two pair LES; prove the every-third-vertical-isomorphism diagram chase from Miller inline. Handle relative covers by quotient/triple exactness. No singular-chain construction is used.

items.title: Skeletal mapping telescope of a cw pair
items.statement: For a CW pair (X,A), put T_X=union over i>=0 of X^i times [i,infinity) in X times [0,infinity), with its CW weak topology, and T_A similarly. Projection gives a map of pairs to (X,A).

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Lemma 2.34, telescope construction p.138
May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§6, telescope construction pp.114–116

items.title: The skeletal telescope projects by a homotopy equivalence of pairs
items.statement: Projection (T_X,T_A) -> (X,A) is a homotopy equivalence of pairs.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Lemma 2.34, complete telescope deformation pp.138–139
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 0.16 p.15 and Theorem A.6 p.524
references.locator: Proposition 0.16 p.15 and Theorem A.6 p.524

items.proof_strategy: Collapse cell prisms in descending dimension, with times accumulating at zero, to obtain compatible filtered slab retractions. Then concatenate slab retractions with times accumulating at one; finite skeleta become stationary. Preserve the subcomplex A throughout.

items.title: A sequential abelian colimit is the cokernel of one minus shift
items.statement: For a sequence of abelian groups G_i and maps u_i, 0 -> direct-sum G_i --(1-s)--> direct-sum G_i -> colim G_i -> 0 is exact, where s sends the ith summand by u_i to i+1.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§6, algebraic lemma p.114
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 3F.8 proof pp.314–315

items.proof_strategy: Injectivity follows recursively from the lowest coordinate of a finite-support vector. The cokernel imposes precisely the generating relations of the colimit; no injectivity of u_i is assumed.

items.title: Additivity and compact cell support control the infinite cw colimit
items.statement: For every ordinary theory with arbitrary additivity, colim_i h_n(X^i,A^i) -> h_n(X,A) is an isomorphism. Consequently the same is true for the directed colimit over all finite subcomplex pairs, and this latter identification is natural for arbitrary continuous maps of CW pairs.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§6, theorem and telescope proof pp.114–116
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 3F.8 pp.314–315

items.proof_strategy: Split the telescope into odd and even cylinder subcomplexes, with intersection the disjoint union of stages. MV and arbitrary additivity identify the overlap map with 1-shift after reindexing; its injectivity kills the next boundary and its cokernel is the colimit. Transfer through the explicit telescope homotopy equivalence. Combine with finite-dimensional finite support, and use compact images to prove continuous-map naturality of the finite-subcomplex colimit.

items.title: Eilenberg steenrod uniqueness on all cw pairs
items.statement: On all CW pairs, a specified coefficient isomorphism determines a unique natural equivalence of ordinary homology theories commuting with boundaries. In particular h with coefficient G is naturally equivalent to singular homology with G.

references.title: May, A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology, 14§6 pp.114–116 and 15§2 pp.119–120
Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology p.161

items.proof_strategy: Extend the finite-dimensional comparison over skeleta and then use finite-subcomplex support for naturality under arbitrary maps. Check compatibility with pair LES and the prescribed coefficient map. Arbitrary additivity is used in the telescope step.

items.title: Degree of a self map of an oriented sphere
items.statement: For n>=1 and f:S^n -> S^n, define deg f in Z by f_*[S^n]=(deg f)[S^n] using integral homology and the same chosen orientation generator on source and target. For two separately oriented sphere copies record both choices.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree, definition p.134

items.title: Degree is homotopy invariant and multiplicative under composition
items.statement: For sphere self-maps in dimension n>=1, homotopic maps have equal degree and deg(g composed with f)=deg(g)deg(f); a homotopy equivalence has degree +/-1.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree properties (c),(d), p.134

items.proof_strategy: Apply the published homotopy and functoriality statements to the chosen integral generator. The converse classification is not part of this proposition.

items.title: Suspension preserves sphere map degree
items.statement: If n>=1, deg(Sigma f)=deg f when the suspension sphere is oriented by the natural suspension isomorphism.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 2.33, p.137

items.proof_strategy: Use the natural suspension square. Specify the unreduced two-cone suspension already used by the library, whose sphere is S^(n+1).

items.title: Degree of identity constant reflection and antipodal sphere maps
items.statement: On S^n, n>=1, identity has degree 1, a constant map 0, a single coordinate reflection -1, and the antipodal map (-1)^(n+1).

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree properties (a),(e),(f) and (b), pp.134–135

items.proof_strategy: For reflection use the oriented boundary of a symmetric simplex (or the two-arc circle computation followed by suspension); swapping two vertices reverses the fundamental cycle. Coordinate reflections are conjugate by orthogonal coordinate changes, and the antipodal is their product.

items.title: A map of nonzero degree between spheres is surjective
items.statement: A continuous map between oriented n-spheres, n>=1, with nonzero degree is surjective.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree property (b), p.134

items.proof_strategy: If a point is omitted, give the stereographic homeomorphism of its complement with R^n and linear contraction; the top homology map factors through zero.

items.title: Local degree at an isolated preimage
items.statement: For f:S^n -> S^n with n>=1, y=f(x), and x isolated in its fibre, choose U containing no other preimage of y. The map H_n(U,U minus {x};Z) -> H_n(S^n,S^n minus {y};Z) is multiplication by the local degree in the generators restricted from the chosen sphere orientations.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Local degree construction, pp.135–136

items.title: Local sphere orientations and finite puncture excision
items.statement: The local groups at sphere points are Z, their orientation generators are restrictions of the global class, and the local degree is independent of shrinking U. For a finite nonempty set F, H_n(S^n,S^n minus F;Z) is the direct sum of these local groups, and the global class maps to their diagonal tuple.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Local-degree diagram and Proposition 2.30 proof, pp.135–136
references.locator: Local-degree diagram and Proposition 2.30 proof, pp.135–136

items.proof_strategy: Use contractibility of a once-punctured sphere and the pair LES, including reduced H_0 for n=1. Excision to disjoint small balls identifies the finite-puncture group. Coordinate projections are inclusions of pairs and send the global class to its restricted local generator; nested excision proves independence.

items.title: Global sphere degree is the sum of local degrees
items.statement: If a value y has finite fibre under f:S^n -> S^n, n>=1, then deg f is the sum of deg_x f over that fibre. The empty fibre contributes zero.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 2.30, p.136

items.proof_strategy: Use the commuting global/relative/local square; the incoming global class is diagonal and the outgoing map adds the local multiples. Treat the empty fibre with the omitted-point lemma.

items.title: Every integer occurs as the degree of a sphere map
items.statement: For each integer d and n>=1 there exists f:S^n -> S^n with deg f=d.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Example 2.31, p.136

items.proof_strategy: For |d| positive pinch the complement of interiors of |d| disjoint disks to a point and fold each disk quotient by an orientation-preserving or reversing homeomorphism. A value away from the pinch point has exactly |d| local contributions of the chosen sign. For d=0 use a constant. This is existence, not classification.

items.title: No retraction from a disk onto its boundary
items.statement: For n>=1 there is no continuous retraction D^n -> S^(n-1).

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Theorem 10.7 proof, p.24

items.proof_strategy: A retraction would split the boundary inclusion on reduced H_(n-1), but the intermediate disk group is zero and the sphere group is Z. Use reduced H_0 when n=1.

items.title: A fixed point free ball map produces a boundary retraction
items.statement: For n>=1, a fixed-point-free continuous f:D^n -> D^n would yield a continuous boundary retraction by following the ray from f(x) through x to the boundary.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Theorem 10.7 proof, p.24

items.proof_strategy: Put v=x-f(x), a=<f(x),v>. The boundary point is f(x)+t v with t=(-a+sqrt(a^2+(1-|f(x)|^2)|v|^2))/|v|^2. Prove v!=0, the chosen root t>=1, continuity on the compact ball, and t=1 when x is on the boundary. This extends the published dimension-two lemma.

items.title: Brouwer fixed point theorem
items.statement: Every continuous self-map of the closed ball D^n has a fixed point for every n>=0.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Theorem 10.7 and proof, p.24

items.proof_strategy: For n>=1 use the ray retraction contradiction. D^0 is a singleton and is handled separately.

items.title: No nowhere zero tangent vector field on an even sphere
items.statement: For positive even n, S^n has no continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field. Here a tangent field is a continuous v:S^n -> R^(n+1) with <v(x),x>=0.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2.28, p.135

items.proof_strategy: Normalize v and use cos(pi t)x+sin(pi t)v(x), whose norm is one, to homotope identity to antipodal; their degrees differ.

items.title: An odd sphere admits a nowhere zero tangent vector field
items.statement: For n=2m-1>=1, identify R^(2m) with C^m; multiplication by i restricts to a continuous unit tangent field x -> ix on S^n.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2.28, positive direction p.135

items.proof_strategy: Check directly that <ix,x>=0 and |ix|=1.

items.title: A sphere has a nowhere zero tangent vector field iff its dimension is odd
items.statement: For n>=1, S^n admits a continuous nowhere-zero tangent field if and only if n is odd.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2.28, p.135

items.proof_strategy: Combine the two established directions; no differentiability is needed.

items.title: A fixed point free sphere map has antipodal degree
items.statement: For n>=1, a fixed-point-free self-map of S^n has degree (-1)^(n+1); therefore every map of any other degree has a fixed point.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree property (g), p.134

items.proof_strategy: The vector (1-t)f(x)-tx never vanishes: a zero at an interior t would force f(x)=x by equal norms. Normalize to homotope f to the antipodal map.

items.title: A group acting freely on a positive even sphere has at most two elements
items.statement: A group acting freely by homeomorphisms on S^(2m), m>=1, has order at most two; if nontrivial it is isomorphic to Z/2.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 2.29, p.135

items.proof_strategy: The degree homomorphism to {+1,-1} has trivial kernel because every nonidentity group element has no fixed point and hence degree -1. The antipodal action realizes the nontrivial case.

items.title: Invariance of dimension for euclidean spaces
items.statement: For nonnegative integers m,n, a homeomorphism R^m -> R^n implies m=n.

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Corollaries 10.5 and 10.6, pp.23–24

items.proof_strategy: Separate dimension zero by cardinality. Puncture corresponding points, translate to zero, and exhibit the radial strong deformation retraction R^k minus {0} -> S^(k-1). Reduced integral homology is supported in exactly degree k-1, including k=1. Do not use invariance of domain.

title: Homology Axioms Degree and Classical Applications — Examples

items.title: Degree of the circle power map
items.statement: For every integer d, the map z -> z^d on the counterclockwise oriented unit circle has degree d, including zero and negative exponents.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Example 2.32, p.137

items.proof_strategy: For d>0 a regular value has d points, each locally an increasing angular homeomorphism. For d<0 compose with complex conjugation/reflection; for zero use the constant map.

items.title: Degree of a coordinate reflection on a sphere
items.statement: A coordinate reflection on S^n has degree -1; exhibit the reversed oriented fundamental cycle in a reflection-invariant triangulation.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree property (e), p.134

items.proof_strategy: Use a symmetric simplex boundary and swap its two opposite vertices; print the cycle/sign calculation rather than simply repeating the proposition.

items.title: Degree of the antipodal map in low dimensions
items.statement: The antipodal maps on S^1,S^2,S^3 have degrees +1,-1,+1 respectively, illustrating the parity distinction in the tangent-field obstruction.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree property (f) and Theorem 2.28, pp.134–135

items.proof_strategy: Compute the number of coordinate reflections in each ambient dimension and relate the odd-dimensional cases to x -> ix.

items.title: Local degrees of a polynomial map on the riemann sphere
items.statement: A complex polynomial P of degree d>=1 extends to an oriented sphere self-map of topological degree d; at a finite point a its local degree is the multiplicity of P(z)-P(a), and at infinity its local degree is d.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 2.30 and Example 2.32, pp.136–137
Lebl, Guide to Cultivating Complex Analysis, Theorem 5.1.3 and Exercise 1.3.9
references.locator: §1.3 stereographic construction and Exercises 1.3.1–1.3.9, pp.19–20; Lemma 5.1.1 and Definition 5.1.2, pp.122–123; Theorem 5.1.3 p.123 read as a stronger comparison, not used.

items.proof_strategy: Construct the sphere model inline: inverse stereographic coordinates send z to (2 Re(z),2 Im(z),|z|^2-1)/(1+|z|^2), and infinity to the north pole; verify continuity and inverse. Use the orientation for which the finite complex coordinate is positive; the infinity coordinate w=1/z has transition derivative multiplication by -1/z^2, hence positive real determinant, or verify its local sign by rotation and positive dilation. Polynomial division gives P(z)-P(a)=(z-a)^m q(z), q(a)!=0. Shrink until |q(z)-q(a)|<|q(a)|, so the straight-line homotopy of q to q(a) never vanishes; this is a homotopy of punctured local pairs to q(a)(z-a)^m. The pair LES identifies its local H_2 action with the angular power map on H_1 of a small circle. Compute the m positive local angular contributions inline, without depending on another B item. At infinity, 1/P(1/w)=w^d/(a_d+a_(d-1)w+...+a_0 w^d), so the same nonvanishing-factor argument gives local degree d. The leading-term growth bound proves extension at infinity. The published polynomial root-multiplicity theorem gives total finite-fibre multiplicity d, and the local-degree sum gives global degree d. This retains all multiplicity conclusions without a holomorphic normal-form or rational-map prerequisite.

items.title: Two homology theories with different coefficient groups
items.statement: Singular homology with Z and with Z/2 both satisfy the ordinary axioms, but cannot be naturally equivalent because their coefficient groups at a point differ.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Axioms for Homology, coefficient discussion p.161
references.locator: Axioms for Homology, coefficient discussion p.161

references.title: Miller, Algebraic Topology I lecture notes, Definition 11.1, p.26

items.proof_strategy: Evaluate any putative equivalence at the point; Z and Z/2 are not isomorphic.

items.title: Degree zero does not imply a sphere map is constant
items.statement: For every n>=1 there is a nonconstant, even surjective, degree-zero self-map of S^n.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Example 2.31, p.136 (signed fold variation)

items.proof_strategy: Pinch two disjoint disks and fold one quotient with local sign +1 and the other with sign -1; outside both disks map to the basepoint. The local-degree sum is zero while each disk quotient surjects. This says nothing against the later nullhomotopy classification.

items.title: Degree is not defined by top homology for self maps of s zero
items.statement: The unreduced top-homology scalar definition does not apply to S^0: H_0(S^0;Z)=Z^2 and the transposition is a nonscalar swap matrix. Reduced H_0(S^0;Z)=Z DOES admit the separate scalar invariant taking values -1,0,+1.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Degree opening paragraph, p.134, excludes n=0
references.locator: Degree opening paragraph, p.134, excludes n=0

items.proof_strategy: Print the identity, swap and two constant matrices in the point basis, and their actions on the difference generator. Exclude only the stated unreduced definition, not every possible notion of degree.

items.title: Finite additivity alone does not prove infinite cw uniqueness
items.statement: Let E_n(X)=(product over i>=0 of reduced H_i(X;Z))/(direct sum over i>=0 of reduced H_i(X;Z)) for every n in Z, and define the relative version similarly. E is a reduced theory satisfying homotopy, exactness, excision, dimension with zero coefficients and finite additivity, but not arbitrary additivity. Thus ordinary H direct sum E agrees with H on every finite-dimensional CW pair and has coefficient Z, yet differs on the wedge of one S^i for every i>=1.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §2.3 Exercise 2, p.165

items.proof_strategy: Construct boundary maps by shifting the graded family of ordinary connecting maps; finite lost end coordinates vanish in product/sum. Prove exactness of the product/sum functor on graded abelian groups by coordinate lifting and finite-support corrections, rather than asserting that quotients of theories are exact. On finite-dimensional CW pairs only finitely many reduced degrees occur, so E=0. On the infinite wedge its value is product Z/direct-sum Z, nonzero via the all-ones class, while E of each sphere is zero. Pass to pairs by the quotient formulation. This is an explicit counterexample to replacing arbitrary by finite additivity.
